title: Gluconeogenesis
objectives: Understand the pathway and significance of gluconeogenesis
Identify key substrates and enzymes involved in glucose synthesis
Explain the regulation of gluconeogenesis and its coordination with glycolysis
Recognize clinical implications of gluconeogenesis dysregulation

overview.title: Pathway Overview
overview.content:
Gluconeogenesis Overview

Gluconeogenesis is the metabolic pathway that synthesizes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors including glucogenic amino acids, lactate, glycerol, and α-ketoacids.

Primarily occurs in liver and kidney, sharing reactions between mitochondria and cytosol.

Biological Significance

  • Maintains blood glucose during fasting/starvation
  • Clears lactate from muscle/RBCs and glycerol from adipose tissue
  • Works with glycogenolysis to prevent hypoglycemia

substrates.title: Substrates
substrates.content:
Gluconeogenic Substrates

1. Glucogenic Amino Acids

Primary Sources: Alanine and glutamine (major glucose source during fasting)

Pathway: Converted to pyruvate → oxaloacetate → PEP

2. Lactate

Source: Exercising muscle and erythrocytes

Conversion: Lactate dehydrogenase converts to pyruvate

3. Glycerol

Source: Adipose tissue TAG hydrolysis

Pathway: Glycerol → glycerol-P → DHAP (bypasses TCA cycle)

4. Propionyl-CoA

Sources: Odd-chain FA β-oxidation, cholesterol side-chain

Pathway: Converted to succinyl-CoA (TCA intermediate)

pathway.title: Pathway Reactions
pathway.content:
Gluconeogenesis Pathway

Key Bypass Reactions

1. Pyruvate → PEP

Step 1: Pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial) converts pyruvate to OAA (requires biotin, activated by acetyl-CoA)

Step 2: PEP carboxykinase converts OAA to PEP (requires GTP, Mg2+)

Transport: Malate shuttle moves reducing equivalents from mitochondria

2. Fructose-1,6-BP → Fructose-6-P

Enzyme: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (rate-limiting, Mg2+-dependent)

Regulation: Inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-BP

3. Glucose-6-P → Glucose

Enzyme: Glucose-6-phosphatase (ER membrane system)

Tissue Specificity: Liver/kidney only (absent in muscle)

Energy Requirements

Consumes: 2 ATP (PC), 2 GTP (PEPCK), 2 ATP (phosphoglycerate kinase), 2 NADH (GAPDH)

regulation.title: Regulation
regulation.content:
Regulation of Gluconeogenesis

1. Glucokinase/Glucose-6-Phosphatase

Glucokinase: Induced by insulin (high glucose)

G6Pase: Induced by glucagon/epinephrine (low glucose)

2. PFK-1/Fructose-1,6-Bisphosphatase

Allosteric: F1,6BPase inhibited by AMP; PFK-1 activated by AMP

F2,6-BP: Activates PFK-1, inhibits F1,6BPase (favors glycolysis)

Xylulose-5-P: Indirectly increases F2,6-BP via PFK-2 activation

3. Pyruvate Kinase/Pyruvate Carboxylase

PK: Inhibited by ATP, acetyl-CoA, LCFA; activated by insulin

PC: Activated by acetyl-CoA (obligatory activator)

PEPCK: Induced by glucagon, epinephrine, glucocorticoids

Futile Cycle Prevention

Reciprocal regulation ensures glycolysis and gluconeogenesis don't occur simultaneously, preventing ATP waste.

clinical.title: Clinical Notes
clinical.content:
Clinical Correlations

Type I Diabetes Mellitus

Pathophysiology:

Insulin deficiency with elevated counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol)

Metabolic Effects:

  • Impaired GLUT-4 translocation → hyperglycemia
  • Activated PEPCK/F1,6BPase → exacerbated gluconeogenesis
  • Increased lipolysis → elevated FFA/glycerol

Treatment Implications:

Insulin therapy required to suppress inappropriate gluconeogenesis

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Why is gluconeogenesis energetically expensive?
It requires 6 high-energy phosphate bonds (4 ATP + 2 GTP) and 2 NADH to synthesize one glucose molecule, compared to glycolysis's net yield of 2 ATP.
How does the malate shuttle benefit gluconeogenesis?
It transports mitochondrial reducing equivalents (NADH) to the cytosol where they're needed for GAPDH reaction, while also moving carbon skeletons.
Why can't muscle perform gluconeogenesis?
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, the final enzyme needed to release free glucose into circulation.
